usage: 보호하다 (保護, 'guard and protect') is the fixed eco verb, never 지키다 alone here.
Shows the non-nature sense: the conditions around you at work.
to be good for the environment
에 marks the thing affected; 환경이 좋다 instead means the place itself is nice.
examples: 저는 환경에 관심이 많아요.
I'm very interested in the environment.
Simple 관심이 많다 = to have much interest; 에 marks the topic of interest.
일회용품을 줄이면 환경을 보호할 수 있어요.
If we cut down on disposables, we can protect the environment.
환경을 보호하다 — the textbook collocation; 줄이다 = to reduce.
이 회사는 근무 환경이 좋아서 직원들이 오래 다녀요.
This company has a good work environment, so employees stay a long time.
Real-situation use of 환경 for workplace conditions, paired with 다니다 (to attend/commute to).
nuance: 환경 is Sino-Korean 環境 ('ring/encircle' 環 + 'boundary' 境), literally the boundary that rings you — hence it covers BOTH the natural environment (nature, pollution, climate) and the human conditions around a person: 근무 환경 (work environment), 가정 환경 (home background). The near-synonym 주변(周邊) means the physical 'surroundings/vicinity' you can point at, while 환경 is the abstract set of conditions that shape you, so a noisy 주변 creates a bad 환경. Register is neutral and works in essays, news, and speech alike; it collocates with 보호하다 (protect), 오염되다 (be polluted), and 파괴하다 (destroy). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: say 환경이 좋다 ('the environment is good') or 환경에 좋다 ('good FOR the environment'), never 환경을 좋다 — 좋다 is an adjective and can't take 을/를.

mistakes: Using 환경 only for nature — it equally means general conditions/surroundings, as in 근무 환경 or 주변 환경; restricting it loses half its range.
Saying 환경을 좋다 — 좋다 is a descriptive adjective, so use 환경이 좋다 (the environment is good) or 환경에 좋다 (good for the environment).
Swapping in 주변 for the abstract sense — 주변 is the visible vicinity, while the set of life conditions is 환경 (가정 환경, not 가정 주변).

usage: 쌓다 ('to stack') is the native verb; 만들다 (make) is wrong for knowledge.
전문(專門) = specialty; standard on résumés and job posts.
풍부하다(豊富) = abundant; a compliment about a well-read person.
What you already know that helps you grasp a new topic.
examples: 저는 역사 지식이 부족해요.
My knowledge of history is lacking.
Simple 부족하다 = to be insufficient; note 지식 takes the topic directly (역사 지식).
책을 많이 읽으면 다양한 지식을 쌓을 수 있어요.
If you read a lot, you can build up varied knowledge.
지식을 쌓다 in an everyday motivational frame; 다양한 = varied.
이 일을 하려면 어느 정도 전문 지식이 필요해요.
To do this job you need a certain level of specialized knowledge.
Real-situation work talk; 어느 정도 = to some degree, 전문 지식이 필요하다 a set phrase.
nuance: 지식 is Sino-Korean 知識 ('to know' 知 + 'recognize/perceive' 識), i.e. accumulated facts and information gained from study or experience. The sharp contrast is with 지혜(智慧) 'wisdom' — the good judgment to USE knowledge well: a scholar may have great 지식 but little 지혜. It also differs from 정보(情報) 'information', which is raw data/news you receive, whereas 지식 is what you've internalized and can apply. Register is neutral-to-formal and fits essays, interviews, and class. The habitual verb is 지식을 쌓다 (picture stacking bricks), and people 풍부하다 in it. English-speaker pitfall: 'knowledge' feels uncountable in English, but Korean freely says 다양한 지식 / 많은 지식, and you never 'make' knowledge (지식을 만들다 ✗) — you accumulate it (쌓다).

Blurring 지식 with 정보 — 정보 is incoming raw data (e.g. 정보를 검색하다), while 지식 is the internalized understanding.

usage: 받다 (receive) is the learner's-side verb — you take education in.
Add 하다 and it's the teacher's-side verb meaning to teach/train.
공(公) = public; contrasts directly with 사교육 (private tutoring).
Common compound when comparing schools or regions.
examples: 저는 좋은 교육을 받고 싶어요.
I want to receive a good education.
Simple 교육을 받다 from the learner's side — note 받다, not 하다.
회사에서 신입 사원을 대상으로 교육을 진행했어요.
The company carried out training for new employees.
Everyday workplace sense; -을 대상으로 = targeting, 진행하다 = to conduct.
한국 부모들은 자녀 교육에 정말 많은 관심을 가져요.
Korean parents take a great deal of interest in their children's education.
Real social topic; 자녀 = one's children (formal), 관심을 가지다 = to take interest.
nuance: 교육 is Sino-Korean 敎育 ('teach' 敎 + 'raise/nurture' 育) — literally to teach-and-rear, so it spans schooling, parenting, and on-the-job training, not just classrooms. The crucial direction split is in the verb: the learner says 교육을 받다 ('receive education'), while the provider says 교육하다 or 교육(을) 시키다 ('cause to be educated'). Near-synonym 훈련(訓練) 'training' is narrower and physical/repetitive (군사 훈련 military training, 직업 훈련 vocational training), whereas 교육 includes intellectual and moral formation. In Korea the 공교육(public) vs 사교육(private cram-school) divide is a constant social theme. English-speaker pitfall: don't say 교육을 하다 when you mean 'to study' — that means you're the one teaching; a student always uses 교육을 받다.

usage: to believe in / practice a religion
믿다 (believe) is the set verb — literally 'to believe a religion'.
Neutral existence frame; the basis of the polite question 종교가 있으세요?
자유(自由) = freedom; appears in civic and constitutional contexts.
Attending services, volunteering, study groups, etc.
examples: 저는 종교가 없어요.
I don't have a religion.
Simple, fully natural answer; 있다/없다 is how Korean frames 'having' a faith.
혹시 믿는 종교가 있으세요?
Do you happen to follow any religion?
Polite real-life question; 혹시 softens it and 믿는 modifies 종교 ('the religion you believe').
한국에서는 다양한 종교가 평화롭게 공존하고 있어요.
In Korea various religions coexist peacefully.
Discussion register; 공존하다(共存) = to coexist, 평화롭게 = peacefully.
nuance: 종교 is Sino-Korean 宗敎 ('ancestral/principal' 宗 + 'teaching' 敎), 'the principal teaching', the general term for religion as a belief system; a religious person is a 종교인. The key contrast is with 신앙(信仰) 'faith/devotion' — 종교 is the institution or category (불교, 기독교 are 종교), while 신앙 is the personal inner belief one holds, so an atheist studies 종교 academically but has no 신앙. Don't confuse 종교 with a specific 교회 (church building / Protestant church) or 절 (Buddhist temple). The verb pair 종교를 믿다 literally 'believe a religion' covers both holding and practicing it. Register is neutral; faith is treated as fairly private, so 종교가 있으세요? is acceptable but not pressed. English-speaker pitfall: never say 종교를 하다 ('do a religion') — you 믿다 (believe) it, or simply 종교가 있다.

usage: 작품(作品) = piece/work; the standard pairing for any art form.
-가(家) makes the practitioner; covers musicians, painters, dancers alike.
전통(傳統) = tradition; e.g. 판소리, 탈춤, crafts.
-적(的) builds the adjective form: 예술적인 감각 (artistic sense).
examples: 저는 예술을 좋아해요.
I like art.
Simple statement; 예술 here means the arts broadly, not just paintings.
이 미술관에서 다양한 예술 작품을 감상할 수 있어요.
At this gallery you can appreciate various works of art.
Everyday outing frame; 감상하다(鑑賞) = to appreciate art, the right verb (not 보다).
요리도 하나의 예술이라고 생각해요.
I think cooking is also a form of art.
Opinion register; 하나의 = 'one (kind of)', a natural way to call something an art.
nuance: 예술 is Sino-Korean 藝術 ('skill/craft' 藝 + 'technique/art' 術), the arts as a whole — 미술(visual art), 음악(music), 무용(dance), 문학(literature), 연극(theatre) all live under it. The sharp contrast is with 미술(美術) 'fine/visual art', which is the narrower branch of painting, drawing and sculpture; a concert is 예술 but not 미술. Don't confuse it with 기술(技術) 'technology/skill', which shares 術 but means practical know-how. Register is neutral and slightly elevated, common in reviews and culture talk; it collocates with 작품 (work), 감상하다 (appreciate), and 표현 (expression). For the adjective, use 예술적(이다) 'artistic', as in 예술적인 표현. English-speaker pitfall: don't make the adjective with 스럽다 — 예술스럽다 ✗; the correct form is 예술적이다 / 예술적인.

mistakes: Using 예술 only for paintings — that narrower visual sense is 미술; 예술 spans music, dance, literature and more.
Saying 예술스럽다 for 'artistic' — the natural adjective is 예술적이다 / 예술적인 (예술적인 감각).
Mixing 예술 with 기술 — both carry 術, but 기술 is practical technology/skill, while 예술 is the creative arts.

usage: 작품(作品) = work; the standard pairing for novels, poems, plays.
Put the nation or era before 문학 to specify the body of work.
고전(古典) = classic; contrasts with 현대 문학 (modern literature).
전공하다(專攻) = to major in; standard academic phrasing.
examples: 저는 문학을 좋아해요.
I like literature.
Simple; here 문학 names the whole field, the academic word for the love of reading-as-art.
이 소설은 한국 현대 문학의 대표 작품이에요.
This novel is a representative work of modern Korean literature.
Everyday review frame; 대표 작품 = representative/landmark work, 현대 = modern.
문학을 통해 그 시대 사람들의 삶을 엿볼 수 있어요.
Through literature you can glimpse the lives of people of that era.
Reflective register; -을 통해 = through, 엿보다 = to catch a glimpse of.
nuance: 문학 is Sino-Korean 文學 ('writing/letters' 文 + 'learning' 學), 'the study of letters' — literature as the art built from language: 소설(novels), 시(poetry), 희곡(drama), 수필(essays). It is one branch under 예술 and is the academic, field-level word, NOT a casual one: to talk about reading for fun, Koreans just say 소설 (novel) or 책 (book), and a single title is a 작품, never '하나의 문학'. The notorious near-miss is 문화(文化) 'culture' — one syllable apart (學 vs 化) but entirely different; '한국 문학' is Korean literature, '한국 문화' is Korean culture. Register is formal/intellectual, fitting essays and university talk. English-speaker pitfall: English 'literature' can loosely mean 'the readings/brochures', but Korean 문학 is strictly the artistic body of writing — product leaflets are 자료/책자, not 문학.

usage: 배우다 (learn) is the natural verb; works for any tongue in the abstract.
외국(外國 foreign) + 어; 어(語) is the bound 'language' suffix.
능력(能力) = ability; very common on résumés and in linguistics.
모국(母國 homeland) + 어 = the language you grew up speaking.
examples: 저는 새로운 언어를 배우고 싶어요.
I want to learn a new language.
Simple goal sentence; 언어 = language as a general concept, 배우다 the right verb.
언어는 그 나라의 문화를 이해하는 열쇠예요.
Language is the key to understanding a country's culture.
Everyday metaphor; 열쇠 = key (figurative), -는 = topic marker on the subject.
그분은 언어 능력이 뛰어나서 통역사로 일해요.
She has excellent language ability, so she works as an interpreter.
Real-situation; 통역사 = interpreter, 뛰어나다 = to be outstanding, -로 marks the job role.
nuance: 언어 is Sino-Korean 言語 ('speech' 言 + 'words/talk' 語), language as the abstract human faculty or any language as a phenomenon. The structural point: a SPECIFIC named language takes the bound suffix 어(語) — 한국어 Korean, 영어 English, 일본어 Japanese — so you STUDY 한국어 but DISCUSS 언어 in general. The casual native near-synonym is 말, which is warmer and also means 'speech/words/remark' (말을 잘하다 = to speak well), whereas 언어 is the technical/written term used in linguistics, policy, and essays. English-speaker pitfall: never glue 언어 onto a country name — '한국언어' ✗ is not a word; the language is 한국어 (country + 어). Also, when you mean everyday 'words' or 'what someone said', use 말, not 언어 (그 말은 상처였어요 = those words hurt).

Sino-Korean 言語 ('speech' 言 + 'words/talk' 語).

Never glue 언어 onto a country name — '한국언어' ✗ is not a word; the language is 한국어 (country + 어). Also, when you mean everyday 'words' or 'what someone said', use 말, not 언어 (그 말은 상처였어요 = those words hurt).

Using 언어 for casual 'words/talk' — that everyday sense is 말 (말이 많다, 좋은 말), while 언어 is the abstract/technical term.
Forgetting 언어 is the general concept — you can't 'speak 언어'; you speak a specific 한국어/영어, and discuss 언어 as a topic.

usage: Describe size with 많다/적다 (many/few), never 크다 (big).
늘다/줄다 for increase/decrease; 늘어나다 is the fuller variant.
감소(減少) = decrease; a flagship social-issue compound.
고령(高齡) = advanced age; pairs in 고령 인구 증가 (rise in the elderly).
examples: 서울은 인구가 많아요.
Seoul has a large population.
Simple; the core lesson — size of 인구 is 많다, not 크다.
요즘 한국은 인구 감소 문제가 심각해요.
These days population decline is a serious problem in Korea.
Everyday news frame; 심각하다(深刻) = to be serious/grave, 인구 감소 a set compound.
이 지역은 젊은 인구가 점점 줄고 있어요.
The young population in this area is gradually shrinking.
Real-situation; 점점 = gradually, 줄다 = to decrease, -고 있다 shows ongoing trend.
nuance: 인구 is Sino-Korean 人口 ('person' 人 + 'mouth' 口) — literally a head-count by 'mouths to feed', the number of people in a place. The decisive collocation rule: its quantity is 많다(many)/적다(few) and its change is 늘다(increase)/줄다(decrease); Korean does NOT use 크다/작다 (big/small), which belong to physical size. Don't confuse 인구 with the look-alike 인기(人氣) 'popularity' (인기가 많다 = popular) or with 식구(食口) 'family members / household mouths', which is the small home unit, not a region's count. Register is neutral-to-formal, dominating demographics and news; today 인구 감소 (decline) and 고령화 (aging) are perennial themes. English-speaker pitfall: 'a big population' tempts 인구가 크다 — wrong; say 인구가 많다.

structuredNuance.t: The number of people in a place. The decisive collocation rule: its quantity is 많다(many)/적다(few) and its change is 늘다(increase)/줄다(decrease); Korean does NOT use 크다/작다 (big/small), which belong to physical size. Register is neutral-to-formal, dominating demographics and news; today 인구 감소 (decline) and 고령화 (aging) are perennial themes.
Don't confuse 인구 with the look-alike 인기(人氣) 'popularity' (인기가 많다 = popular) or with 식구(食口) 'family members / household mouths', which is the small home unit, not a region's count.
Sino-Korean 人口 ('person' 人 + 'mouth' 口) — literally a head-count by 'mouths to feed'.
'A big population' tempts 인구가 크다 — wrong; say 인구가 많다.

mistakes: Saying 인구가 크다 — population is counted, so use 인구가 많다/적다 (many/few), not 크다/작다 (big/small).
Confusing 인구 (population) with 인기 (popularity) — they look alike but 인기가 많다 means 'is popular', unrelated to headcount.
Mixing 인구 with 식구 — 식구 is the members of one household ('우리 식구는 네 명'), while 인구 is a region's total people.

usage: Common demonstrative + 지역, for any defined locale.
주민(住民) = residents; the set pairing in civic talk.
사회(社會) = society; 지역 사회 = the local community as a whole.
수도권(首都圈) = the greater-Seoul metropolitan zone.
examples: 이 지역은 조용해요.
This area is quiet.
Simple description; 지역 as a neutral 'area' you can point to on a map.
지역마다 사투리와 음식이 조금씩 달라요.
Dialects and food differ a little from region to region.
Everyday observation; 지역마다 = every region, 사투리 = dialect, 조금씩 = bit by bit.
지역 주민들이 환경 보호 활동에 적극적으로 참여했어요.
Local residents actively took part in environmental protection activities.
Civic-news register; 적극적으로 = actively, 참여하다 = to participate, -에 marks the activity.
nuance: 지역 is Sino-Korean 地域 ('land/earth' 地 + 'boundary/territory' 域), a bounded geographic area, and by extension the 지역 사회 (local community). Two contrasts matter. Against 지방(地方) 'the provinces': 지역 is any neutral region (수도권 지역 included), whereas 지방 specifically means everywhere OUTSIDE Seoul (지방에 살다 = to live in the provinces), often with a center-vs-rest nuance. Against 동네: 지역 is formal/administrative (지역 경제, 지역 주민), while 동네 is your warm, familiar block where neighbors know you. Register is neutral-formal, common in news and policy. English-speaker pitfall: 'I'm from the countryside/regions' becomes 지방, not 지역; and your cozy neighborhood is 동네, so '우리 동네' (my neighborhood) sounds natural where '우리 지역' would feel like a press release.

mistakes: Confusing 지역 (any neutral region/area) with 지방 — 지방 specifically means the provinces outside the capital ('지방 출신' = from outside Seoul).
Using 지역 for your cozy neighborhood — that warmer, personal sense is 동네 (우리 동네 빵집).
Saying 지역이 크다 for community closeness — for a tight-knit local society use 지역 사회, and describe size of land with 넓다 (wide), not just 크다.

usage: Add 하다 for the act: 전화를 발명하다 (to invent the telephone).
품(品) = item; the physical thing that was invented.
-가(家) makes the person who invents; 에디슨은 발명가예요.
위대하다(偉大) = great; standard praise for a landmark creation.
examples: 전화는 위대한 발명이에요.
The telephone is a great invention.
Simple; 발명 as the noun for a created thing, framed with 위대한 (great).
에디슨은 전구를 발명한 것으로 유명해요.
Edison is famous for inventing the light bulb.
Everyday fact frame; -(으)ㄴ 것으로 유명하다 = to be famous for having done.
그 학생은 재미있는 발명품을 만들어서 상을 받았어요.
That student made an interesting invention and won a prize.
Real-situation; 발명품 (the invented item) is what you 만들다, then 상을 받다 = win a prize.
nuance: 발명 is Sino-Korean 發明 ('emit/bring forth' 發 + 'bright/clear' 明), 'to bring something into the light' — creating a device or method that did not exist before, with 발명품 being the resulting product. The essential contrast is with 발견(發見) 'discovery' ('emit' 發 + 'see' 見): you 발명하다 a telephone (made new) but 발견하다 a planet or a law of nature (already there, newly found). Register is neutral, common in history, science and patents; it collocates with 발명가 (inventor), 발명품 (the product), and 특허 (patent). English-speaker pitfall: keep act vs object straight — the abstract act/concept is 발명/발명하다, but the physical gadget you hold is a 발명품, so '재미있는 발명을 만들다' is odd; say '재미있는 발명품을 만들다'. Also don't reach for 발견 (discover) when nothing pre-existed.

mistakes: Confusing 발명 (invention — creating something new) with 발견 (discovery — finding what already existed) — you 발명하다 a machine but 발견하다 a fossil.
Saying 발명을 만들다 for a physical item — the made object is 발명품, so 발명품을 만들다; 발명하다 alone is the act.
Using 발견 for human-made things — a new app or recipe is 발명/개발, not 발견.

usage: Add 하다 for the act of coming across or realizing something.
새로운 = new; the staple pairing in science writing.
우연하다(偶然) = by chance; 우연히 발견하다 (find by chance).
Passive 되다 when the discoverer is unknown or unstated.
examples: 과학자들이 새로운 행성을 발견했어요.
Scientists discovered a new planet.
Simple active sentence; 발견하다 with a clear agent (scientists) and object (planet).
그 그림은 한 농부에 의해 우연히 발견되었어요.
That painting was discovered by chance by a farmer.
Everyday passive; -에 의해 = by (agent), and 발견되다 backgrounds the finder.
여행하면서 나 자신에 대한 새로운 점을 발견했어요.
While traveling, I discovered something new about myself.
Figurative real-situation; 발견하다 = to realize, -에 대해 = about, 새로운 점 = a new aspect.
nuance: 발견 is Sino-Korean 發見 ('emit/bring forth' 發 + 'see' 見) — to bring into sight something that already existed but was unknown: a planet, an old manuscript, even a fresh truth about yourself. The pivotal contrast is with 발명(發明) 'invention', which CREATES the never-before-existing (telephone, light bulb), whereas 발견 only uncovers what was there. The verb 발견하다 stretches figuratively to 'realize/notice' (새로운 면을 발견하다 = to discover a new side of someone). Register is neutral, frequent in science, news and reflection; it collocates with 새로운 (new), 우연히 (by chance), and the passive 발견되다. English-speaker pitfall: when no agent is named, English keeps active voice ('they found...'), but Korean prefers the passive 발견되다 (유물이 발견되었다 = artifacts were discovered); and don't use 발견 for human creations — those are 발명.

usage: 발달하다(發達) is the idiomatic verb for tech progress, not 자라다.
Fixed pairing in news, policy and R&D talk.
Shows the hands-on sense: a practical, learnable craft.
최신(最新) = newest; standard product/marketing phrasing.
examples: 요즘 기술이 빠르게 발달해요.
These days technology develops quickly.
Simple; the core collocation 기술이 발달하다 with 빠르게 (quickly).
그는 요리 기술이 뛰어나서 유명한 식당에서 일해요.
He has outstanding cooking skills, so he works at a famous restaurant.
Everyday personal-skill sense; here 기술 = hands-on technique, not high-tech.
새로운 기술 덕분에 많은 일이 자동화되고 있어요.
Thanks to new technology, many tasks are being automated.
Real-situation; -덕분에 = thanks to, 자동화 = automation, -고 있다 ongoing change.
nuance: 기술 is Sino-Korean 技術 ('skill/ability' 技 + 'technique/art' 術), and it straddles two senses context disambiguates: macro-level technology (과학 기술, IT 기술, 최신 기술) and an individual's practical skill or technique (요리 기술, 운전 기술). Contrast with 예술(藝術), which shares 術 but is the creative arts, and with 능력(能力) 'ability/capacity', which is innate or general capability rather than a trained, specific technique — a person has 능력 broadly but acquires a concrete 기술. Register is neutral. The collocations split by sense: technology 발달하다 (advances) or 발전하다, while a person 기술을 배우다/익히다 (learns/masters). English-speaker pitfall: 'technique improved' tempts 기술이 발전되다 for a person, but for an individual's skill say 기술이 늘다 (skill grows); reserve 발달/발전 for technology at large.

mistakes: Using 기술 only for high-tech — it equally means a hands-on personal craft (요리 기술, 운전 기술).

Mixing 기술 with 능력 — 능력 is general capacity/ability, while 기술 is a specific learned technique ('운전 능력' is your overall driving capacity, '운전 기술' the concrete maneuvering skill).

usage: Add 하다 for sustained academic/scientific investigation.
결과(結果) = result; the standard outcome pairing.
진행하다(進行) = to carry out/proceed with a study.
원(員) = staff member; the person who does the research.
examples: 저는 한국어를 연구해요.
I research the Korean language.
Simple; 연구하다 frames deep, systematic study — heavier than '공부해요'.
이번 연구 결과가 학계에서 큰 주목을 받았어요.
These research findings drew great attention in academia.
Everyday academic frame; 학계 = academic world, 주목을 받다 = to draw attention.
대학원에서 한국어 교육에 대해 연구하고 있어요.
I'm researching Korean language education in graduate school.
Real-situation; -에 대해 = about/on, 대학원 = grad school, -고 있다 ongoing project.
nuance: 연구 is Sino-Korean 硏究 ('grind/hone' 硏 + 'investigate to the end' 究) — to grind away at a question until you reach its depths, i.e. systematic academic or scientific research aimed at producing NEW knowledge. The decisive contrast is with 공부(工夫) 'studying': you 공부 a textbook to absorb what's already known (for an exam), but you 연구 a problem to discover what isn't yet known — a grad student 공부하다 coursework yet 연구하다 a thesis. Near-synonym 조사(調査) is narrower 'survey/investigation' (설문 조사 = questionnaire survey, 경찰 조사 = police inquiry), a fact-finding step rather than the whole scholarly enterprise. Register is formal/academic, clustering with 연구실 (lab), 연구원 (researcher), 연구 결과 (findings). English-speaker pitfall: don't use 연구 for everyday schoolwork ('I studied for the test' = 공부했어요, not 연구했어요), and findings 'come out' — 연구 결과가 나오다 — rather than being 'made'.
